::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## For instructors: how this page is built
The lesson is a single `.qmd` file. A setup script in the front matter prepares the VM
before any window attaches — every student starts from exactly the same state, and a
reload gives them a fresh machine:

```yaml
quarto-os:
  vm:
    setup: |
      git config --global user.name "Ada Lovelace"
      git config --global user.email "ada@example.com"
      git config --global core.pager cat
      mkdir -p ~/project && cd ~/project
      cat > README.md <<'EOF'
      # Recipes
      …
      EOF
```

The workspace on the right is three windows in a CSS grid (sticky while you scroll),
and each step uses run snippets like `` `git status`{.os-run target="git"} ``:

```markdown
::: {#code .os-window app="vscode" folder="~/project" open="pancakes.md"}
:::
::: {#files .os-window app="explorer" path="~/project"}
:::
::: {#git .os-window app="terminal" cwd="~/project"}
:::
```
:::

## 0 · Your workspace

On the right you have three windows, all looking at the **same** Linux machine:

- **VS Code** — an editor with the project's files.
- **Explorer** — the folder `~/project`, *including hidden files*.
- **Terminal** — a `bash` shell in `~/project`. This is where we type git commands.

Click a grey command to run it in the terminal, or type it yourself. The machine is
already prepared: a folder `~/project` with two files, and git knows your name:

`git config --global --list`{.os-run target="git"}

::: {.look}
Two files in the Explorer: `README.md` and `pancakes.md`. No `.git` folder yet — this is
just a normal folder.
:::

## 1 · Is this a repository?

`git status`{.os-run target="git"}

Git answers `fatal: not a git repository`. A folder only becomes a repository when we
ask for it.

## 2 · Create a repository

`git init`{.os-run target="git"}

::: {.look}
A **`.git`** folder appears in the Explorer. *This* is the repository: git's whole
database lives in there. Your files next to it are just the "working tree".
:::

Have a peek inside — what's on the current branch?

`ls .git`{.os-run target="git"} · `cat .git/HEAD`{.os-run target="git"}

## 3 · What does git see?

`git status`{.os-run target="git"}

::: {.look}
Both files are **untracked**: git sees them, but doesn't manage them yet. In VS Code,
open the **Source Control** view (the branch icon on the left): the files are marked
**U** for untracked.
:::

## 4 · Stage a file

Committing is a two-step process. First we choose what goes into the next commit by
adding it to the **staging area**:

`git add README.md`{.os-run target="git"} then `git status`{.os-run target="git"}

::: {.look}
`README.md` is now listed under *Changes to be committed*. In the Explorer, a new file
**`.git/index`** appeared — that *is* the staging area.
:::

## 5 · Your first commit

Stage the other file too and save a snapshot with a message:

```{.bash .os-run target="git"}
git add pancakes.md
git commit -m "Add README and pancake recipe"
```

Older git versions call the first branch `master`; let's rename it to `main` and look
at the history:

```{.bash .os-run target="git"}
git branch -M main
git log
```

::: {.look}
The commit has an id (a long hash), an author — the name from the setup — and a date.
Open `.git/objects` in the Explorer: git stored your files there, compressed. The
Source Control view in VS Code is empty again: nothing has changed since the commit.
:::

## 6 · Change something

Our pancakes need more sugar. Edit `pancakes.md` in **VS Code** — change `1 tbsp sugar`
to `2 tbsp sugar` and save with <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>S</kbd> — or let `sed` do it:

```{.bash .os-run target="git"}
sed -i 's/1 tbsp sugar/2 tbsp sugar/' pancakes.md
```

Now ask git what changed:

`git status`{.os-run target="git"} · `git diff`{.os-run target="git"}

::: {.look}
`git diff` shows the old line with `-` and the new one with `+`. VS Code marks
`pancakes.md` with **M** (modified) — click it in the Source Control view to see the
same diff side by side.
:::

Stage and commit in one go (`-a` stages all *tracked* files that changed):

`git commit -am "More sugar"`{.os-run target="git"}

## 7 · Branches

A branch is a movable label on a commit. Let's try a waffle recipe without touching
`main`:

`git checkout -b waffles`{.os-run target="git"}

::: {.look}
In the Explorer, open `.git/refs/heads`: there's a file per branch, `main` and
`waffles`. And `cat .git/HEAD`{.os-run target="git"} now points to `waffles`.
:::

Add a recipe and commit it on the branch:

```{.bash .os-run target="git"}
printf '# Waffles\n\n- 250 g flour\n- 2 eggs\n- 400 ml milk\n' > waffles.md
git add waffles.md
git commit -m "Add waffle recipe"
```

## 8 · Switch back

`git checkout main`{.os-run target="git"}

::: {.look}
**`waffles.md` disappears** from the Explorer and from VS Code! It isn't lost: it lives
in the `waffles` branch. Checking out a branch makes the working tree look like that
branch's latest commit.
:::

`git log --oneline --graph --all`{.os-run target="git"}

## 9 · Merge

Happy with the waffles? Bring the branch into `main`:

`git merge waffles`{.os-run target="git"}

::: {.look}
Git reports a **fast-forward**: `main` simply moved up to the waffle commit, and
`waffles.md` is back. The graph is a straight line again:
`git log --oneline --graph --all`{.os-run target="git"}
:::

## 10 · Challenge: a merge conflict

What if two branches change the *same line*? Make one branch use oat milk while `main`
reduces the milk:

```{.bash .os-run target="git"}
git checkout -b oat-milk
sed -i 's/300 ml milk/300 ml oat milk/' pancakes.md
git commit -am "Use oat milk"
git checkout main
sed -i 's/300 ml milk/250 ml milk/' pancakes.md
git commit -am "Less milk"
git merge oat-milk
```

::: {.look}
`CONFLICT (content)`. Open `pancakes.md` in VS Code: git wrote **both** versions into
the file between `<<<<<<<`, `=======` and `>>>>>>>` markers. Decide what the recipe
should say (`250 ml oat milk`?), delete the markers and save.
:::

Then tell git the conflict is resolved and finish the merge:

```{.bash .os-run target="git"}
git add pancakes.md
git commit --no-edit
git log --oneline --graph --all
```

## Done!

You used `init`, `status`, `add`, `commit`, `log`, `diff`, `branch`, `checkout` and
`merge` — and saw what each one does to the files and to `.git`.

- Want to start over? **Reload the page** — you get a fresh machine.
